source.version: Published conference proceedings version: Proceedings of the 59th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, 2026; printed pp. 95-103. The proceedings identification and year appear in the footer of PDF p. 1.
source.title_on_document: The Confidence Cage: How Creative Self-Efficacy Hinders Gen AI-Augmented Ideation

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is mentioned in the full PDF. The results tables and figures are in the main paper (PDF pp. 5-7, Tables 1-3 and Figures 1-2); the document ends with references (PDF pp. 8-9).

paper_design_summary: Prolific adults completed a baseline Alternative Uses Test for a fork and were then randomly assigned to use either a custom GPT-4o brainstorming coach or a text-only web search engine while generating uses for a Frisbee (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2). The analysis included 300 people, 150 per arm, after exclusions; a language-model scoring system evaluated their output with a composite creativity score (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1 and 3.3; p. 6, Table 2). Self-reported ideation and baseline creative self-efficacy were used in mediation and moderation analyses (PDF pp. 5-7, Sections 3.3-4 and Table 3).

studies.label: Online experiment: GPT-4o coaching versus web search on alternative uses

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were assigned after the baseline fork task to Human-AI or Human-Search for the Frisbee post-test. Condition was between participants, and pre-test versus post-test was within participants; the paper describes a 2 × 2 mixed factorial design. Assignment concerned AI assistance to people, not the source of independently generated AI versus human outputs.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of two conditions for the post-test task with control.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 98), Sections 3.1 Design and participants and 3.2 Procedure.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement or registration link is given in the full PDF; methods are on PDF pp. 4-5, Sections 3.1-3.4.

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: Custom GPT-4o chatbot available during the post-test, asking probing questions and offering perspectives without direct task solutions. Copy-paste was disabled; participants were instructed to use it as a collaborative thinking tool (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2). The arm count is the final analyzed count (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 2).

arms.name: Human-Search
arms.description: Custom text-only web search engine available during the post-test, intended for inspiration; visual stimuli were eliminated and the same copy-paste restriction applied (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2). The arm count is the final analyzed count (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 2).

participants.exclusions: 327 people were recruited, and 27 were excluded from analyses: verbatim copying of complete internet responses (n = 15), failure to follow instructions (n = 8), incomplete task completion (n = 3), and chatbot system error (n = 1). The final sample was 300, with 150 per arm. The paper does not separately give the number randomized before exclusions or exclusions by arm; recruited and final analyzed counts are not coded as randomized counts (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).
participants.who: Adults recruited through Prolific; eligibility required age at least 18, English fluency, and residence in the United States or Canada (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1).
participants.quote: The final sample included 300 participants, with 150 assigned to each experimental condition.
participants.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 98), Section 3.1 Design and participants; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 100), Table 2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 101), Table 3 note (N = 300).

ai_tool.name_model: Custom chatbot powered by OpenAI's GPT-4o API (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: During the Frisbee AUT, the chatbot asked probing questions and offered new perspectives to stimulate divergent thinking, without providing direct solutions. Copy-paste was disabled and participants were instructed to treat it as a collaborative thinking tool. The intervention model is identified, but an exact dated model snapshot and the system prompt are not provided (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).

task.description: Guilford Alternative Uses Test: generate as many creative and unusual uses as possible for a fork at baseline and a Frisbee at post-test, emphasizing novelty and practicality. The baseline task preceded assignment, and the assigned aid was used during the post-test (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.2-3.3).
task.duration: 5 minutes for each AUT task; approximately 25-30 minutes for the online session (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).

outcomes.name: Post-test Alternative Uses Test composite creativity score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: An LLM-based automated system, citing Organisciak et al. (2023), evaluated novelty, usefulness, and divergence from typical applications and produced a composite creativity score (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3, continuing on p. 5). Separate component scores are not reported. The reported analyses use participant creativity scores; the exact scoring model/version, scale, and method of aggregating multiple uses into a participant score are not specified. This is the main H1 endpoint, but no formal primary-outcome designation is stated (PDF p. 3, H1; p. 5, Section 4). Unadjusted and baseline-adjusted comparisons, pre/post displays, and mediation/moderation analyses concern this same outcome and are retained together (PDF pp. 5-7, Tables 1-3 and Figure 1). The post-test is performed with the assigned tool available, not after removal of AI (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2).

contrasts.reported: Unadjusted post-test, Table 2: Human-AI n = 150, M = 3.21, SD = 0.22; Human-Search n = 150, M = 2.98, SD = 0.31. Baseline values in the same table: Human-AI M = 2.94, SD = 0.37; Human-Search M = 2.85, SD = 0.38 (PDF p. 6, Table 2). ANCOVA controlling for baseline creativity, age, work experience, gender, and race: F(1, 293) = 58.28, p < .001, η²p = .166. The results prose gives adjusted Human-AI M = 3.19, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [3.15, 3.24], versus Human-Search M = 2.99, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [2.95, 3.04]; adjusted mean difference = 0.20 points and Cohen's d = 0.77. R² = .251, adjusted R² = .235 (PDF p. 5, Section 4). SOURCE CONFLICT: Table 2 instead prints adjusted Human-Search M = 3.19 [3.15, 3.24] and Human-AI M = 2.99 [2.95, 3.04], reversing the arm labels relative to the results prose. Both versions are retained as printed. The coded direction follows the unadjusted values, results prose, and Figure 1, not the contradictory adjusted column (PDF pp. 5-6, Section 4, Table 2 and Figure 1). Path analysis: direct condition effect on creativity after accounting for ideation B = 0.169, SE = 0.032, z = 5.25, p < .001; Table 3 gives 95% CI [0.110, 0.232]. Ideation-to-creativity path B = 0.030, SE = 0.012, z = 2.50, p = .013; Table 3 gives 95% CI [0.009, 0.055]. Creativity-model R² = .298. Table 3 also reports Condition × MOD for the creativity outcome: B = 0.051**, SE = 0.016, 95% CI [0.004, 0.104], where ** denotes p < .01 (PDF p. 6, Section 4 and Table 3; p. 7, Table 3 note). Indirect condition effect on creativity through self-reported ideation: B = 0.031, SE = 0.013, z = 2.38, p = .017, 95% CI [0.010, 0.062]. Conditional indirect effects: low CSE (−1 SD), B = 0.040, SE = 0.017, z = 2.40, p = .016, 95% CI [0.013, 0.080]; mean CSE, B = 0.031, SE = 0.013, z = 2.38, p = .017, 95% CI [0.010, 0.062]; high CSE (+1 SD), B = 0.021, SE = 0.010, z = 2.18, p = .029, 95% CI [0.006, 0.050]. Index of moderated mediation B = −0.008, SE = 0.004, z = −2.05, p = .040; Table 3 gives 95% CI [−0.021, −0.001]. High-minus-low difference B = −0.019, SE = 0.009, z = −2.05, p = .041; Table 3 gives 95% CI [−0.048, −0.003] (PDF p. 6, Section 4 and Table 3). The methods specify 5,000 bootstrap samples and 95% bias-corrected intervals for mediation (PDF p. 5, Section 3.4).
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 99), Sections 3.4 and 4; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 100), Table 2 (embedded image checked visually), Figure 1, results prose and Table 3; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 101), Table 3 note.

eligibility.reason: All three criteria are met in S1. Individuals were randomly assigned to a generative-AI coach or an active web-search control while performing a creative task (PDF p. 4, Sections 3.1-3.2). There were 300 people analyzed, 150 per arm, after exclusions (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 6, Table 2). Their generated uses received an automated composite creativity score (PDF p. 4, Section 3.3, continuing on p. 5). This supports with_ai with an ai_vs_active contrast; it is not AI-generated output versus human-generated output and is not an after_ai assessment. The conflict in adjusted arm means is flagged for extraction but does not alter design eligibility.

one_line_finding: Among 300 analyzed participants, GPT-4o coaching improved automated AUT creativity relative to web search (unadjusted M = 3.21 versus 2.98; reported adjusted Cohen's d = 0.77), although Table 2 reverses the adjusted arm means in the results prose (PDF p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Table 2).
open_questions: Which adjusted arm means are correct? PDF p. 5, Section 4 assigns 3.19 [3.15, 3.24] to Human-AI and 2.99 [2.95, 3.04] to Human-Search, whereas PDF p. 6, Table 2 assigns them to the opposite arms. The form preserves both without correcting the publication.

How many of the 327 recruited participants were randomized before exclusions, and how were exclusions distributed across conditions? PDF p. 4, Section 3.1 gives recruitment and final analyzed counts but no separate initial assignment counts.

What exact scoring model/version, response aggregation rule, and score scale produced the participant creativity composite? PDF p. 4, Section 3.3 describes LLM scoring and cites Organisciak et al. (2023) without these details.
Which standard deviation was used for the reported Cohen's d = 0.77? PDF p. 5, Section 4 reports it for the adjusted mean difference but does not identify the standardizer.
notes: Screened independently as B on 2026-10-09. Locators use one-based PDF pages, with printed proceedings page numbers supplied where helpful. Read the full markdown conversion and all PDF pages; inspected the embedded images for Tables 1-2 and Figures 1-2 and extracted Table 3 directly from the PDF. Outcome inventory: Table 1 (PDF p. 5) reports pre-test and post-test creativity, pre-test and post-test self-reported ideation, and baseline creative self-efficacy, alongside demographic and condition variables. Figure 1 and Table 2 (PDF p. 6) report the same creativity outcome at baseline and post-test. Table 3 (PDF pp. 6-7) models post-test ideation and creativity and gives conditional indirect effects. Figure 2 (PDF p. 7) depicts predicted self-reported ideation by condition and creative self-efficacy. Only the composite creativity score is an outcome scored on participant output. Ideation is a self-report adapted from the Runco Ideational Behavior Scale, and CSE is a baseline self-report moderator (PDF p. 5, Section 3.3); neither is coded as output fluency, flexibility, or creativity. No separate novelty, usefulness, or divergence estimates are given despite these being components of automated scoring. Baseline creativity is retained within the same outcome as a covariate/descriptive measure, not counted as an additional study or an after_ai outcome. The paper reports no across-person diversity measure and no later unassisted assessment. Conditional indirect effects describe mediation through self-reported ideation; they are not separate observed creativity outcomes or subgroup total treatment effects. No eligible output outcome was omitted. No data or code availability URL is stated in the document. No effect sizes, standard errors, or other numerical estimates were computed for this form.
